items.followUp: Define root hairs and state how they help a plant absorb water and minerals.

rubric.why: Identifies root hairs as extensions of root epidermal cells.
rubric.description: Root hairs are tiny tubular extensions of the epidermal cells of roots.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying root hairs as extensions of root epidermal cells.

rubric.why: States the role of root hairs in absorption.
rubric.description: They increase the root’s surface area and absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that root hairs increase surface area for absorbing water and/or mineral salts.

modelAnswer: Root hairs are tiny tubular extensions of the epidermal cells of roots.
They increase the root’s surface area and absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.

items.followUp: Explain how light energy is absorbed and used during photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Identifies chlorophyll as the green pigment found in chloroplasts.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in chloroplasts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying chlorophyll as the green pigment in chloroplasts.

rubric.why: States that chlorophyll captures light energy.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy needed for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll absorbs light energy.

rubric.why: Explains light’s role as an energy source or its effect on the process.
rubric.description: Light provides energy for photosynthesis, and its intensity affects the rate of the process.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying light as the energy source or stating that light intensity affects the rate.

rubric.why: Connects light energy to chemical energy and food production.
rubric.description: Absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy and used to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that light energy is converted or used to produce glucose.

rubric.why: Gives a relevant detail about the wavelengths absorbed or reflected by chlorophyll.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light or reflects green light.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in chloroplasts.
It absorbs light energy needed for photosynthesis.
Light provides the energy for photosynthesis, and its intensity affects the rate of the process.
The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy and used to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light.

items.followUp: Describe how sugars move from a source to a sink through phloem by the pressure-flow mechanism.

rubric.why: Identifies sugar loading at the source.
rubric.description: Sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem at a source, such as a leaf.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugar is loaded into the phloem at the source.

rubric.why: Explains water entry and the resulting pressure rise at the source.
rubric.description: Water enters the phloem from the xylem by osmosis, raising hydrostatic pressure at the source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing water entry by osmosis and its effect on pressure.

rubric.why: Explains movement of phloem sap down a pressure gradient.
rubric.description: The pressure difference causes phloem sap to flow by mass flow towards a sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking a pressure difference or gradient to mass flow towards the sink.

rubric.why: Describes sugar unloading and its fate at the sink.
rubric.description: At the sink, sugars are unloaded and used or stored.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugars are unloaded at the sink and used or stored.

accept: pressure is lower at the sink
pressure is lower at the sink
rubric.why: Completes the pressure-flow cycle at the sink.
rubric.description: Water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, so pressure is lower at the sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing water leaving the phloem and returning to the xylem, or for stating that pressure is lower at the sink.

modelAnswer: At the source, such as a leaf, sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem.
Water enters the phloem from the xylem by osmosis, raising the hydrostatic pressure at the source.
The pressure difference causes phloem sap to flow by mass flow towards a sink.
At the sink, sugars are unloaded and are used or stored.
Water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, so pressure is lower at the sink.
